# Total War and the Institutional Filter {#sec-3-09}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act III — Hoover, War, and the Archive State · 1939–1941
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** How does crisis select for ecosystems?

**The answer.** It picks winners by geography and readiness. Rearmament money
did not spread evenly; it went where engineering schools, laboratories, and
industrial capacity already sat next to each other. California's advantage was
not destiny. It was that when the money started moving, the state already had
the three things the money needed in the same place.

**The mechanism.** Public subsidy about to be converted, and the selection stage
of the conversion. The chapter's discipline is anti-determinist: California was
chosen, by identifiable people applying identifiable criteria, and it could have
been chosen otherwise.

**The key fact.** Hewlett-Packard was founded in a garage at 367 Addison Avenue
in Palo Alto in 1939 with about five hundred dollars. The garage is the founding
image of the American technology industry, and its first significant customer
base was the war.

**The human anchor.** Two of Terman's students in a rented garage, choosing to
stay in California when the entire electronics industry was on the east coast —
because their professor told them to.

**Excluded voices.** Japanese Americans in California, whose incarceration from
1942 is part of this period and belongs in this act rather than only in Act V's
ledger. The farms and businesses lost are a transfer of assets, and the transfer
had beneficiaries.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that California's technological primacy was
selected rather than inevitable by showing the specific institutional and
geographic criteria that federal science funding applied before 1941.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

Two of Frederick Terman's students rented a garage at 367 Addison Avenue in Palo
Alto in 1939 and started a company with about five hundred dollars. The chapter
uses the most famous image in American business history and then deflates it:
the garage matters because of what was already around it, and specifically
because a professor had told them to stay.

The deflation is the point. Every electronics company of consequence was on the
east coast in 1939, and Hewlett and Packard remained in California on Terman's
advice — the first appearance of the man who allocates talent, and the first
demonstration that the allocation is deliberate. Their early business was
instruments, and their early customers were substantially military.

The chapter's main work is anti-deterministic. Rearmament money from 1938 onward
did not spread evenly across the country; it went where laboratories,
engineering schools, and industrial capacity already sat next to one another,
and it was directed by identifiable people applying identifiable criteria.
California was behind at that point. MIT and Harvard captured the major early
contracts, and nothing about the outcome was obvious in 1940. The state's
advantage was readiness rather than destiny: a growing technical education base,
industrial capacity, and the Pacific — geography becoming an asset for the first
time since Spain claimed the Bay in Act II.

That contingency makes the eventual result more interesting rather than less.
The corridor was selected, and it could have been selected elsewhere.

The chapter also places Japanese American incarceration here, in 1942, rather
than deferring the whole subject to Act V's ledger. Farms, businesses, and homes
were lost, and property that is lost is property that someone else acquires. The
transfer had beneficiaries, and the chapter names the mechanisms.

By 1941 the state is positioned and the money is about to arrive in quantities
nobody has seen. The next chapter is about the man who had a plan for it.
:::

:::

::: {.chapter-question}
How does crisis select for ecosystems?
:::

In 1939 two of Frederick Terman's former students rented a garage behind a house
at 367 Addison Avenue in Palo Alto and started a company with about five hundred
dollars.

The garage is now a California state landmark with a plaque calling it the
birthplace of Silicon Valley. It is a small wooden structure behind an ordinary
house on an ordinary street, and it is worth visiting for the deflation.

Because the garage is not the explanation. Two engineers in a shed are a common
occurrence and they usually produce nothing. What made this one consequential is
everything that was already around it, and the first item on the list is that
their professor had told them to stay.

## Terman's advice

William Hewlett and David Packard were Stanford engineering graduates. In 1939
the American electronics industry was on the east coast — RCA, General Electric,
Bell Laboratories, and the radio manufacturers — and a young engineer with
ambition went east, as almost all of Terman's best students had.

Terman told them not to. He had a view, which he had been developing for some
years, that California could sustain a technical industry of its own, and that
the reason it had not was that the region kept exporting its graduates. He
provided encouragement, a small loan, and access to the university's facilities.

The point is not the loan. It is that a professor was functioning as an
allocator of talent, deliberately, against the prevailing gradient, and that he
understood this as a strategy rather than as mentorship. Act IV's first chapter
is about what happened when he applied the same logic with an industrial park
behind it.

Hewlett-Packard's first product was a resistance-capacitance audio oscillator,
based on Hewlett's graduate work, and its first significant customer was Walt
Disney, which bought eight of them for the sound system used with *Fantasia*.
Within two years the customer base was substantially military, and that is the
transition this chapter is about.

## The selection

Rearmament money began moving in the United States from around 1938, and it did
not spread evenly. It went where three things already sat close together:
engineering schools capable of producing and holding technical staff,
laboratories with equipment and a research culture, and industrial capacity able
to manufacture at scale.

Those criteria were applied by identifiable people. The National Defense
Research Committee, established in 1940 under Vannevar Bush, and the Office of
Scientific Research and Development that succeeded it in 1941, made decisions
about which institutions received contracts. Bush was an MIT man. The largest
wartime research contracts went to MIT, to Harvard, to Caltech, and to Bell
Laboratories.

Stanford did not get them. This is the fact that keeps this chapter honest, and
it is the fact the standard Silicon Valley origin story omits entirely.

In 1940 Stanford was a good regional university with a strong engineering
department and no particular claim on the national scientific establishment.
California was a large agricultural state with an aircraft industry in the south
and a naval presence around the Bay. The proposition that the San Francisco
Peninsula would become the centre of the world's technology industry would have
struck an informed observer in 1940 as eccentric.

The outcome was not fated. It was selected, later, by people applying criteria,
and it could have been selected otherwise. Boston very nearly kept it, and for a
period after the war Route 128 was ahead.

## What California did have

Geography, for the first time since Spain claimed the Bay in Act II chapter 2.

The Pacific war made the west coast the theatre's logistical base. Shipyards at
Richmond, Sausalito, and Vallejo. Aircraft manufacturing in southern California
at a scale that reorganised the region's economy. Naval installations around the
Bay, and Moffett Field in Sunnyvale, which had been built for airships in the
1930s and became an aeronautical research centre.

It also had a growing technical education base at Stanford, Berkeley, and
Caltech, and a population that was about to increase very rapidly.

Readiness, not destiny. The distinction is the chapter's whole argument.

## Berkeley, and the other California

One institution did receive an enormous wartime commission, and it was not
Stanford.

Ernest Lawrence's Radiation Laboratory at Berkeley had built cyclotrons through
the 1930s on foundation money, and when the Manhattan Project needed to separate
uranium isotopes at scale, Lawrence's electromagnetic method became one of the
principal approaches. The laboratory expanded enormously. Los Alamos was
directed by Berkeley's J. Robert Oppenheimer.

Berkeley demonstrates that California could host science at the highest level
and that federal money would go there when the case was strong enough. It also
demonstrates the model Terman would later copy: a laboratory whose scale
depended on federal contracts, attached to a university, with a director who
functioned as an entrepreneur.

Stanford watched this happen to its neighbour, and its dean of engineering spent
the war somewhere else thinking about it.

## Incarceration

One further event of this period belongs in this act rather than deferred to Act
V's ledger, because it happened here and it was an asset transfer.

Executive Order 9066, signed in February 1942, led to the forced removal and
incarceration of some hundred and twenty thousand people of Japanese ancestry
from the west coast, roughly two-thirds of them United States citizens. They
were given days or weeks to dispose of homes, farms, and businesses.

The economic consequence was a transfer. Property was sold at distress prices,
abandoned, or lost for non-payment during the years of absence, and it was
acquired by people who remained. Japanese-American farmers had, despite the
Alien Land Law of 1913 described in Act II chapter 11, built substantial
holdings in California agriculture, and much of it did not come back.

This is the same mechanism the whole act has been describing, running at speed
and under wartime authority: a population with no political standing supplies
something valuable, and its removal has beneficiaries who are not required to
account for the gain.

## The other filter

Federal money was not the only thing selecting for California in these years.
People were arriving, and the arrival was itself a selection.

The Second World War produced the largest internal migration in American
history. Something in the region of a million and a half people moved to
California during the war years to work in shipyards, aircraft plants, and the
supporting economy, and among them were several hundred thousand Black Americans
leaving the South in the second Great Migration. Richmond's population
multiplied several times over in four years around the Kaiser shipyards.

The industries that recruited them did so under federal pressure. Executive
Order 8802, in 1941, prohibited discrimination in defence industries and
established the Fair Employment Practice Committee, after A. Philip Randolph
threatened a march on Washington. It was the first federal action of its kind
since Reconstruction, and it worked partly because the labour shortage was
acute.

What it did not touch was housing, and the housing regime was the one described
in chapter 3: restrictive covenants in the deeds, redlining in the federal
underwriting maps, and public war housing that was segregated and largely
temporary. Workers recruited into the wartime economy were confined to
neighbourhoods that could not expand and could not accumulate equity, and when
the shipyards closed the jobs went and the restrictions stayed.

The chapter's point is that the wartime expansion of California was federally
directed in both dimensions at once. The same government that required
industries to hire without discrimination was simultaneously insuring mortgages
on terms that made segregation a condition of lending.

Act IV chapter 1 will describe a research park whose workforce could live in
Palo Alto. This is why the question of who could live there has an answer.

## Positioned

By the end of 1941 California is positioned and the money is about to arrive in
quantities nobody has previously seen.

The state is not yet the centre of anything. Its principal university is not in
the front rank of the wartime research effort. Its most famous technology
company is two men and a garage with a few dozen employees.

What it has is geography, capacity, a technical education base, and a dean of
engineering who is about to spend three years running an eight-hundred-person
laboratory at Harvard and take detailed notes on how the money works.
